title: The Getaway: photographing, rebuilding and streaming ten square miles of London on PS2
summary: Team Soho turned location photography, custom tools and aggressive streaming into a recognizable London whose roads guided both driving and crime drama, years before city-scale photogrammetry became routine.

sourceLabels.playstation-retrospective: The Getaway Turns 15: A Look Back With the Team Behind the PS2 Hit
sourceLabels.content-acquisition: London Wasn't Built in a Day: Content Acquisition for Levels in The Getaway

blocks.text: A driving prototype expanded into a city drama

The project began from ideas related to Porsche Challenge, then grew into a narrative-led crime game in which London itself would carry equal weight with the cast. Team Soho committed to a free-roaming urban area rather than disconnected tracks. That decision multiplied the requirements for road continuity, landmarks, traffic, interior transitions and story staging on hardware with no hard drive.

Artists systematically photographed streets, shop fronts, signs, junctions and surface details. Overcast weather was useful because it reduced hard shadows that would conflict with the game's lighting. The photographs were not pasted into a map automatically. They were reference and texture material that had to be catalogued, corrected, compressed and interpreted by artists building a coherent virtual district.

Reproducing every facade at equal fidelity would have exhausted memory and schedule. Major landmarks, road proportions, lane markings and characteristic shop rows received the detail needed for recognition, while less important structures could be simplified. The result pursued geographic credibility rather than a survey-grade twin. Players needed to believe a route through London while driving at speed, not inspect every window from centimetres away.
The city had to stream from an optical disc

The PS2 could not hold the map in memory, and the retail machine offered no mandatory hard disk. Geometry, textures, traffic and mission objects had to arrive from DVD as the player moved. Road layout therefore served two jobs: it represented London and gave the streaming system time to prepare what lay around bends, intersections and interior entrances.
Custom tools kept a large art team moving

The content-acquisition account describes artists exporting and playing the game repeatedly from shared development systems. Fast iteration mattered because a correction could affect navigation, collision, visibility and streaming boundaries at once. Tooling was not an invisible convenience; it determined whether the team could maintain a city whose many pieces had to agree under continuous traversal.
Minimal navigation made the road language visible

Instead of covering the screen with a conventional minimap, the game used the vehicle's indicators to suggest turns. Damage was communicated through smoke, handling and character movement rather than a permanent health bar. The restrained interface supported the cinematic goal, but it also placed unusual pressure on route cues, camera behavior and the player's ability to read real road geometry.

Performed scenes, licensed vehicles and a tightly authored crime narrative shared space with traffic and free driving. Missions had to preserve dramatic timing even when a player collided, missed a junction or arrived from an unexpected angle. The city was not merely a background between cutscenes; it was the variable stage on which authored sequences had to survive player deviation.
Emulation exposes streaming and presentation assumptions

Testing should include long, fast drives across district boundaries, repeated interior entries, cutscene transitions and sudden route reversals. Optical-disc timing changes can reveal pop-in or pauses that original scheduling hid. Correct aspect ratio, field rendering, motion blur and audio streaming matter because the game's realism depends more on a stable photographic whole than on any single high-resolution texture.
Why its London remains historically important

The Getaway shows how an ambitious city was built before automated capture pipelines and abundant memory. Location crews, artists, tool programmers and mission designers converted a real place into a constrained streaming system. Its rough edges are inseparable from that scale, but so is its achievement: a recognizable capital functioning as road network, film set and technical budget at the same time.
